summary: The process in RFC 6761 for registering special-use domain names has run into unexpected difficulties in practice. This memo lists the problems found so far in an attempt to be comprehensive, and discusses what needs to be addressed.

eli5.summary: Some names are set aside for special jobs, but the sign-up process turned out to be confusing. This lists everything that went wrong.

questions: why is special-use domain name registration difficult
subtitle: When a process for reserving special domain names breaks down

tldr.problem: RFC 6761 created a process for registering domain names for special technical purposes, but in practice this process has run into many unexpected problems during application.
tldr.mechanism: This document comprehensively lists the 21 problems that have surfaced, from lack of coordination between IETF and ICANN to confusion about what counts as a "technical use" to the simple difficulty and delay of the registration process itself.
tldr.outcome: The document is informational and does not propose solutions, but establishes a clear record of issues that need to be addressed by whoever undertakes to fix or replace the RFC 6761 process.

today: RFC 8244 is an Informational document published in October 2017. It remains the authoritative enumeration of problems with the RFC 6761 process and has not been superseded. Work on improving or replacing the special-use domain name registration process continues in the IETF DNSOP Working Group.

sections.title: The Special-Use Domain Names Process
sections.content:
Domain names are the symbolic addresses that direct traffic on the Internet. RFC 6761, published in 2013, established the IANA "Special-Use Domain Names" registry and the process for adding domain names to it when they serve technical purposes rather than being ordinary addresses people can register.

The process worked in theory: if new functionality requires special handling of a domain name, an IETF Standards Action or IESG Approval must be published describing it. The registry then records the designation with a pointer to the section defining how that name should be handled.

However, as the IETF has attempted to designate new special-use names in recent years, a wide variety of unexpected problems have emerged. This document enumerates them comprehensively to inform future work on improving or replacing the process.
sections.eli5: The IETF has a way to officially claim special domain names for special jobs, like .local. The way it was supposed to work looked simple on paper, but actually trying to use it revealed lots of problems nobody expected.

sections.title: The 21 Problems Identified
sections.content:
The document identifies 21 distinct problems, ranging from structural and policy issues to practical implementation difficulties.

Coordination and authority problems: There is no formal process for the IETF and ICANN to coordinate on name allocations. Both organizations claim authority over the domain namespace, but neither can enforce that authority against third parties who simply start using names. The term "technical use" has no precise definition.

Process problems: Assigning the first special-use name (.local) through the RFC 6761 process took over ten years, creating a justified perception that the process is slow and difficult. In some cases the IETF has made special-use assignments without following the process at all (treating guidance as requirements, or failing to add the name to the registry afterward).

Protocol and naming problems: When a new special-use name is designated, not all software that processes domain names will understand its special meaning, so queries for it may leak to the public DNS root servers. There is demand for multiple name resolution protocols beyond DNS, but there is no mechanism to identify which protocol should handle a given name. Some names are used both in the DNS and as special-use names, creating ambiguity.

Registry and documentation problems: Some RFCs add entries to the registry when they designate special-use names, while others do not. There is no safe, non-process-violating mechanism for ad hoc assignment. The DNSSEC handling of special-use domain names is an open question.
sections.eli5: The document lists problems in every direction: nobody knows who is in charge, the process takes forever, software doesn't understand the special names, and there is no way to document names that leak out even though nobody planned for them to be special.

sections.title: Historical Context and Existing Practices
sections.content:
To understand why special-use domain names exist at all, the RFC reviews the history of name resolution on the Internet. Before the DNS, hostnames were resolved using a central HOSTS.TXT file. When that became impractical, the DNS emerged as the standard, but other protocols (NetBIOS Name Service, Sun's Network Information System) also competed and left their mark on how systems resolve names.

The document notes that many modern operating systems can still use /etc/hosts files, name service switches to resolve some domains differently, and mDNS (Multicast DNS) for .local names. This history explains why protocol developers choose to use domain names even for alternative resolution systems: domain names are required in so many contexts (user interfaces, APIs) that developers have little choice but to claim a special name from the domain namespace.

RFC 6761 itself recognizes several types of special-use names: those used solely with DNS with no special handling; those resolved using DNS but requiring special handling in resolvers; and those requiring special handling in stub resolvers, like .local. The document discusses liaison statements, memoranda of understanding (RFC 2860) between IETF and ICANN, and various secondary documents (Multicast DNS, .onion, Name Collision in the DNS) that illustrate the practical issues.
sections.eli5: Before the Internet had a unified way to look up names, everyone was making up their own systems. That history is why people still want special domain names today, and why the IETF and ICANN have complicated overlapping claims to control them.

sections.title: Why This Matters Now
sections.content:
RFC 8244 is informational, not standards-track, and proposes no solutions. However, it serves as essential required reading for anyone in the IETF who wishes to participate in discussions about special-use domain names. The document establishes that the problems identified are real and interconnected.

The document reflects broad disagreement about the validity of some of the problems and about which organizations (IETF, ICANN, IANA, or others) should address them. It explicitly takes no position on these points. Instead, it provides the context necessary for productive future discussion of solutions, regardless of which organization ultimately undertakes that work.
sections.eli5: This document doesn't fix anything, but it lists all the broken parts clearly so that whoever does try to fix things later will understand what they are working with.
